advisor.summary: Section 280A(g) draws a bright statutory line: rent a residence for fewer than 15 days in the year and the rent never enters gross income, with the owner-side deductions denied in exchange. Pair that exclusion with a §162(a) rent deduction at the entity level, and the client's business can pay documented fair-market rent to hold genuine meetings — planning days, board sessions, trainings — in the owner's home, deducting what the owner collects tax-free. The structure is neither novel nor contested; the government litigates price and proof. Sinopoli shows the Tax Court honoring the framework while slashing rents that lacked comparables and meeting evidence, and §280A(a) closes the door on a sole proprietor renting from themselves. The ceiling is modest by design — a clean four-figure play, not a centerpiece.
mechanics: The §280A(g) exclusion operates per dwelling unit used as a residence: stay under 15 rental days for the year and no rent is includible, though owner-side rental deductions are barred; the fifteenth day is a cliff that makes every rental dollar received that year taxable.

The entity's side of the transaction rests on §162(a): the rent must be ordinary, necessary, and reasonable in amount — which in practice demands a genuine, documented business reason for each individual rental day.

Price from daily-event comparables — hotel conference rooms, coworking event space, banquet rooms of similar capacity — refreshed annually and retained in the file; dividing monthly residential rent by thirty is the method Sinopoli punished.

Each rental day needs its own contemporaneous evidence package built to §274-style discipline: agenda or notice, minutes or work product, attendee list, an owner-to-entity invoice, and a traceable payment.

A Schedule C business cannot run this play: with no separate payor, the owner is renting from themselves, and §280A(a)'s general disallowance leaves nothing deductible — an S corporation, partnership, or C corporation tenant is a structural prerequisite.

authority.note: The statutory core: the under-15-day exclusion paired with its companion denial of owner-side deductions.
Governs the entity's rent deduction; the standard demands both reasonableness in amount and a business purpose.

The court left the structure intact but cut roughly $3,000-per-meeting rents to about $500 where the taxpayers offered no comparable-rate support and thin proof the meetings occurred. The lesson is evidentiary, not structural.
The general disallowance that defeats the self-payor variant and keeps sole proprietorships out.
The contemporaneous-documentation discipline examiners borrow when testing each rental day's business purpose.

requirements: A separate business entity — S corporation, partnership, or C corporation — serving as the paying tenant.
No more than 14 rental days per residence per year, tracked on a hard calendar.
A genuine business event on each rented day, evidenced by agenda, minutes, and attendee list.
A written owner-to-entity invoice and an actual, traceable payment for every rental.
A current comparable-rate file supporting the daily rate, refreshed each year.
risks: Rate inflation is the leading audit theory: Sinopoli v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2023-105, is the template — unsupported premium rents re-set to a small fraction on exam — and any rate the comparables file cannot carry should expect the same haircut.
A drumbeat of recurring board meetings at a single-owner entity, with no minutes and no work product, invites disallowance of the entire deduction plus accuracy-related penalties.
One day too many kills the year: at 15 rental days the §280A(g) exclusion vanishes and every rental dollar becomes taxable.
The dollars are inherently small — never let a client defend an aggressive rate or a padded calendar over a four-figure benefit.
Careless overlap with a claimed home-office use pattern can undermine both positions; reconcile the rented spaces and days.
stateNotes: Conformity: states that start from federal AGI inherit the exclusion automatically; verify any non-conformity or addback states in the client's footprint before presenting the number as fully tax-free.

PTET interaction: the rent is an ordinary entity deduction, so it already reduces the income base on which a pass-through entity tax election is computed — the engine sequences PTET after this deduction, and no separate state benefit should be layered on top.
Missouri: conforms through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121) with no addback for §280A(g) amounts, so the excluded rent stays off the Missouri return as well.
reviewChecklist: Payor entity exists, is in good standing, and is not simply the client's own Schedule C activity.
Daily rate is anchored to at least two current local daily-use comparables retained in the file.
Planned day count is 14 or fewer and plausible against the client's actual business calendar.
Documentation kit (agenda, minutes, invoice, payment method) is issued and the client has acknowledged the commitments in writing.
Modeled benefit uses the client's true marginal rate and does not double-count the PTET effect.
No conflict with a claimed home-office deduction pattern covering the same spaces and days.

client.teaser: Your business pays for meeting space anyway — this makes you the landlord, and the rent is tax-free.
client.headline: Rent your home to your business — up to 14 tax-free days a year
plainEnglish: The tax code has a rule nicknamed the Augusta Rule. It is named for homeowners in Augusta, Georgia, who rent out their houses each year during the Masters golf tournament. If you rent your home to anyone for 14 days or fewer in a year, the rent you collect is not taxed. It does not even go on your return.

Your business already holds real meetings — annual planning, team training, board sessions. Instead of paying a hotel for a conference room, the business can rent your home for those days at the local going rate. The business deducts the rent as a normal expense. You keep the money and pay no tax on it.

What keeps it safe is routine, not clever moves. Hold real meetings. Use the agenda and minutes templates we give you. Charge a rate backed by real local quotes. Stop at 14 days. We set up every piece and check the count at year-end.
client.analogy: The conference-room bill your business would have paid a hotel now comes to your own front door — and unlike almost any other money you can receive, it arrives untaxed.
benefits: Up to 14 days of rental income each year, tax-free to you
Your business deducts the full rent
Nothing extra to file — just clean records
steps: WE gather real quotes from local meeting venues and set a supportable daily rate.
WE build your meeting calendar and hand you the agenda, minutes, and invoice templates.
YOU hold the meetings for real and fill in the short minutes each time.
YOU have the business pay the rent by check or transfer — never cash — and stop at day 14.
clientCommitments: Hold the meetings for real — the paperwork must describe something that happened
Fill in the one-page minutes at each session
Never let the rental count go past 14 days in a year
Keep every payment traceable from the business account to yours

annualMaintenance: Refresh the comparable-rate quotes each year
Track the rental-day count and enforce the hard stop at 14
Year-end reconciliation of invoices, minutes, and payments
deliverables: Corporate resolution authorizing home rentals for stated business purposes
Comparable-rate memo with retained venue quotes
Meeting agenda, minutes, and invoice templates
Annual rental summary schedule for the file

suggest.reason: A separate payor entity can rent the owner's home for up to 14 days of documented business use.

reviewTriggers: New case law applying or limiting §280A(g)
